question:
A 49-year-old woman presents to the primary care physician with complaints of recurrent episodes of right upper abdominal pain for the past 2 years. She is currently symptom-free. She mentions that the pain often occurs after a heavy fatty meal and radiates to her right shoulder. On examination, the patient has no tenderness in the abdomen and all other systemic examination is normal. Blood work shows:
Leukocyte count 8,000/mm³
Total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL
Prothrombin time 12 s
Aspartate transaminase 58 IU/L
Alanine transaminase 61 IU/L
Serum albumin 4.1 g/dL
Stool occult blood negative
Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows a thickened gallbladder wall with few gallstones. A hydroxy iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan was done which demonstrated non-filling of the gallbladder and a minimal amount of tracer in the common bile duct. Which of the following best describes a histopathological feature in the gallbladder described in this case?

options.opa: Neutrophilic infiltration with vascular congestion and fibrin deposition in the gallbladder
options.opc: Entrapped epithelial crypts seen as pockets of epithelium in the wall of the gallbladder
options.opd: Hyalinized collagen and dystrophic calcification in the submucosal layer
options.ope: Abnormal deposits of cholesterol ester in macrophages in the lamina propria

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Gallstones -> Gallbladder wall thickening -> Non-filling of gallbladder on HIDA scan -> Minimal tracer in common bile duct -> 80%
enhanced_information: The histopathological feature in the gallbladder described in this case is likely to be neutrophilic infiltration with vascular congestion and fibrin deposition, consistent with acute cholecystitis associated with gallstones.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is acute cholecystitis associated with gallstones, as indicated by the patient's symptoms, imaging findings, and HIDA scan results. The enhanced information supports the histopathological feature of neutrophilic infiltration with vascular congestion and fibrin deposition in the gallbladder. This pattern is consistent with acute cholecystitis. The other options are less likely based on the clinical presentation and test results.
